# Slide-by-Slide Inventory: AI Deep Learning Program, Sessions 1–6

All files located in `/Users/davidohara/develop/improving/AI-Course-Development/AI-Deep-Learning-Program/Trainer/Training-Sessions/`.

---

## Session 1 — SDLC Skeletons + Epics & Stories (Week 1, Loop 1, Role Focus: Product/Process)

| # | Type | Description |
|---|------|-------------|
| 1 | Intro | Frames the session: see the full SDLC pipeline, learn Prompt/Harness/Model, build the epics-and-stories skill. |
| 2 | Check-In | "When you use AI today, what exactly are you using? Where does the AI end and your tool begin?" — primes the Prompt/Harness/Model distinction. |
| 3 | Session Goals | Four goals: understand Prompt/Harness/Model; see the 7-skill SDLC pipeline; build epics-and-stories via RTCC + EDD; write EC before building. |
| 4 | Lecture | **Prompt/Harness/Model framework** — Prompt = instructions; Harness = the capability boundary (what the model can do on your machine; Claude Code/Devin/Copilot/ChatGPT as examples); Model = the intelligence that cannot act beyond the harness. |
| 5 | Lecture | **Skill files with `disable-model-invocation: true`** — every program artifact is an RTCC skill file, started with explicit slash-command invocation only; auto-invocation deferred to Session 5. |
| 6 | Lecture | **The SDLC Pipeline** — the 7 skeleton skills (create-prd → create-architecture → create-ux → create-epics-stories → plan-story → implement-story → review-implementation), all RT-only stubs; YAML pipeline handoff (`stories.yaml` written by step 4, read by step 5). |
| 7 | Demo | RT-only skeleton outputs — runs create-prd/architecture/ux against the "Pantry Tracker PWA" to show plausible-but-gappy output when Context/Constraints are empty. |
| 8 | Lecture | **RTCC prompt structure** — Role (WHO), Task (WHAT), Context (WHY), Constraints (HOW), and why the ordering matters (purpose before data). |
| 9 | Lecture | **EDD: define Evaluation Criteria before you build** — EC-first discipline; EC (quality bar for skill output) vs. AC (criteria inside each story) distinction. |
| 10 | Compare/Contrast | **Basic Prompting vs. DLP Completion** — ad-hoc prompts vs. committed RTCC skills; "seemed better" vs. EC-first evaluation; shareable artifacts; documented iteration. |
| 11 | Demo | **Good/bad/AI-generated story contrast** — three sample-stories examples: good (clear testable AC, edge cases), vague (plausible but untestable), AI-generated-without-care (implementation detail like PostgreSQL/JWT/Redux in AC, oversized epics). |
| 12 | Exercise | Lab 1: IDE Setup + Rules File (20 min) — configure agentic IDE, commit a project-level rules file. |
| 13 | Exercise | Lab 2: Write EC for the Epics-and-Stories Skill (15 min) — 4–6 measurable EC committed before building. |
| 14 | Exercise | Lab 3: Build Out the Epics-and-Stories Skill (45 min) — fill Context/Constraints in the skeleton; first application of the Load-Bearing Rule; writes `stories.yaml`. |
| 15 | Exercise | Lab 4: Evaluate, Audit, and Iterate (20 min) — group EC scoring; **load-bearing audit**: remove instructions that map to no EC, re-run to verify scores hold. |
| 16 | Lecture | **Baseline Self-Assessment** — AI Adoption Maturity Assessment, 21 questions × 7 dimensions, A–D scoring (21–84); value is Week 7/12 comparison. |
| 17 | Closing | Recap of the four goals, framed per role (Product/Process, Development, Testing). |

## Session 2 — The Development Loop (Week 3, Loop 1, Role Focus: Development)

| # | Type | Description |
|---|------|-------------|
| 1 | Intro | Plan → Code as the inner development loop; callout that Session 1's `stories.yaml` is Session 2's input (garbage in, garbage out). |
| 2 | Check-In | How has the epics-and-stories skill performed? EC scores, failures, fixes — connects stories to plans. |
| 3 | Session Goals | Four goals: build plan-story skill; build implement-story skill; understand the plan quality dependency; write EC for both skills first. |
| 4 | Lecture | **The Development Loop** — Plan → Code → Evaluate → Iterate; plan-story reads `stories.yaml`/writes `plan.yaml`; implement-story takes the *plan* (not the story) as its specification; fix the plan, not the code. |
| 5 | Lecture | **Plan Failure Modes** — vague plans, missing edge cases, over-specification, story disconnect (no AC reference), scope creep. |
| 6 | Compare/Contrast | **Direct Code (Basic Prompting) vs. The Development Loop (DLP Discipline)** — "write the code" vs. plan-then-generate; the plan as a reviewable artifact; thinking separated from generating. |
| 7 | Demo | The Development Loop on a real story — plan-story then implement-story; shows specific-vs-vague plan effect on code quality. |
| 8 | Exercise | Lab 1: Write EC for Plan and Code Skills (15 min) — 4–6 EC per skill, committed before building. |
| 9 | Exercise | Lab 2: Build Out the Plan-Story Skill (45 min) — RTCC build-out, Load-Bearing Rule, writes `plan.yaml`, tested on sample stories. |
| 10 | Exercise | Lab 3: Build Out the Implement-Story Skill (30 min) — generates code from the plan as input (the discipline), EC evaluation. |
| 11 | Exercise | Lab 4: **The Plan Quality Dependency** (20 min) — run vague vs. improved story through Plan → Code; group analysis; conclusion that quality problems trace upstream. |
| 12 | Closing | Recap of the four goals per role. |

## Session 3 — Review Implementation (Week 5, Loop 1, Role Focus: Testing)

| # | Type | Description |
|---|------|-------------|
| 1 | Intro | Closes Loop 1 by building review-implementation, the final skill in the SDLC pipeline. |
| 2 | Check-In | Development Loop results; did you observe vague plans → vague code? |
| 3 | Session Goals | Four goals: build review-implementation; write review EC first; see the full Loop 1 chain assembled; understand what reviews cover that code/tests don't. |
| 4 | Lecture | **What a Review Covers (and What AI Can and Can't Do)** — **review-implementation feedback loop**: reads `stories.yaml` + `plan.yaml` + code, writes `review.yaml`, and updates `stories.yaml` (`review_status`, `review_notes`); humans prioritize, AI accelerates enumeration; AI failure modes (over-flagging, missing business risk). |
| 5 | Lecture | **Review-Implementation RTCC structure** — concrete R/T/C/C for the review skill (senior reviewer role; severity levels; must reference affected AC item). |
| 6 | Compare/Contrast | **Code (Session 2) vs. Review (Session 3)** — "does it implement the plan?" vs. "does it satisfy the story?"; developer-owned vs. testing-owned; working code vs. issues/severity/recommendations. |
| 7 | Demo | Review on a real story — full chain visible for the first time; watch for over-flagging and missed business risks. |
| 8 | Exercise | Lab 1: Write EC for the Review Skill (15 min) — 4–6 EC committed before building. |
| 9 | Exercise | Lab 2: Build Out the Review-Implementation Skill (45 min) — RTCC build-out, Load-Bearing Rule, writes `review.yaml` and updates `stories.yaml`. |
| 10 | Exercise | Lab 3: **Load-Bearing Audit + Full Pipeline Assembly** (30 min) — audit the review skill; walk one story through the entire Loop 1 chain end-to-end; observe the review feedback loop into `stories.yaml`. |
| 11 | Lecture | **Loop 1 Retrospective** — "In Week 1 I couldn't ___, now I can ___"; previews Sessions 4 (Python evals/LLM judges), 5 (model invocation/adversarial agents), 6 (bounded agents/custom harness). |
| 12 | Closing | Recap of the four goals per role. |

## Session 4 — EDD with Python Evaluations (Week 7, Loop 2, Role Focus: Product/Process)

| # | Type | Description |
|---|------|-------------|
| 1 | Intro | Makes evaluation systematic: **deterministic checks first (fast, free, structural), LLM judges second (qualitative judgment)**; Python scripts drive iteration. |
| 2 | Check-In | "Did you change a skill? How do you know the change made it better — or just different?" — exposes intuition-vs-measurement gap. |
| 3 | Session Goals | Four goals: articulate EDD (Red/Green/Refactor for skills); write a Python eval script with LLM judge; run a documented hypothesis → change → measure → conclude cycle; apply the Refactor step to remove dead instructions. |
| 4 | Lecture | **EDD: Red, Green, Refactor for skills** — precise TDD analogy (Red = baseline EC failures; Green = one hypothesized change until EC pass; Refactor = remove instructions whose deletion fails no EC); **one change per iteration** rule. |
| 5 | Lecture | **The LLM Judge pattern** — **deterministic first, LLM judge second** (schema validation, field counts, format patterns before any model call); 6-step judge pattern; why LLM judges over string matching; why Python over YAML config tools. |
| 6 | Lecture | **Structured output from LLM judges** — judge returns JSON (criterion / pass / score / reasoning, overall_score); enables aggregation across inputs, score history, before/after comparison, improvement reports. |
| 7 | Compare/Contrast | **Informal Evaluation vs. EDD with Deterministic Checks + LLM Judges** — "it seemed better" vs. documented per-EC scores, baselines, one-change iterations, committed eval script + improvement log. |
| 8 | Demo | Python evaluation with LLM judge — script loads skill output, runs deterministic checks then LLM judge, produces structured per-EC report vs. baseline. |
| 9 | Exercise | Lab 1: Write a Python Evaluation Script with LLM Judge (45 min) — 4–6 EC as code (deterministic + judge), 3 test inputs, deterministic-only baseline first, then judge. |
| 10 | Exercise | Lab 2: Baseline, Hypothesize, Iterate (35 min) — one documented EDD cycle: hypothesis, single change, before/after scores, conclusion. |
| 11 | Exercise | Lab 3: Document the Improvement Cycle and Refactor (30 min) — committed improvement log; evaluator-driven load-bearing refactor. |
| 12 | Closing | Recap of the four goals per role. |

## Session 5 — Model Invocation + Adversarial Agents (Week 9, Loop 2, Role Focus: Development)

| # | Type | Description |
|---|------|-------------|
| 1 | Intro | Two new questions: when should the model auto-invoke a skill, and how do you challenge AI output with AI. |
| 2 | Check-In | What did the Python evaluator reveal? Which instructions were dead weight? |
| 3 | Session Goals | Four goals: apply the three graduation criteria; enable model invocation or document the gap; write an adversarial agent prompt; understand how adversarial agents complement Python evaluation. |
| 4 | Lecture | **Model Invocation: Flipping the Switch — the three graduation criteria**: (1) exact triggering inputs agreed in writing, (2) output specification, (3) at least 3 verified positive trigger test cases (invocation + output quality); criterion 3 is the most important; the harness controls invocation, not the model. |
| 5 | Lecture | **Adversarial Agents: AI Challenges AI** — definition (a prompt that attacks another skill's output); **the two-prompt problem** (worker prompt + evaluator prompt both need vetting — "vet the vetted"); how it differs from Python evaluation ("what did the EC miss?"); the 5-step pattern; **good-prompt criteria: calibrated severity (blocker/major/minor/nit) and specific actionable findings**. |
| 6 | Lecture | **How Adversarial Agents relate to the Prompt/Harness/Model framework** — the harness passes the primary skill's output to the adversarial prompt; the model supplies judgment; in the IDE it's a `disable-model-invocation: true` skill, in a custom harness (Session 6) it runs automatically. |
| 7 | Compare/Contrast | **Python Evaluation (Session 4) vs. Adversarial Agents (Session 5)** — known-EC measurement vs. unanticipated-problem discovery; retrospective vs. proactive; deterministic+judge vs. fully AI; "does it meet the criteria?" vs. "what did the criteria miss?" |
| 8 | Exercise | Lab 1: Graduation Criteria for Model Invocation (30 min) — apply the three criteria; enable invocation (commit 5 test cases: 3 positive trigger, 2 quality) or document the specific gap. |
| 9 | Exercise | Lab 2: Write an Adversarial Agent Prompt (40 min) — adversarial skill targeting one existing skill; document at least one issue the Session 4 evaluator missed. |
| 10 | Exercise | Lab 3: Connect Your Evaluator and Your Adversarial Agent (30 min) — map EC ↔ adversarial findings; promote findings to new EC; document the delta. |
| 11 | Closing | Recap of the four goals per role. |

## Session 6 — Bounded Agents, Custom Harness Demo & Stage 4 Preview (Week 11, Loop 2, Role Focus: Testing)

| # | Type | Description |
|---|------|-------------|
| 1 | Intro | Build a bounded agent (chained skills in the IDE), watch a custom-harness demo, locate yourself at IIOS Stage 3, preview Stage 4, close the program. |
| 2 | Check-In | Did anyone enable model invocation since Session 5 — did it fire/silence correctly? Can you describe your most-run skill's invocation boundary? |
| 3 | Session Goals | Four goals: build a bounded agent (full pipeline in one IDE session); see the custom-harness demo; understand the IIOS stage framework (Stage 3 now, Stage 4 next); complete capstone, final assessment, commitment statements. |
| 4 | Lecture | **Bounded Agents: multi-step orchestration in the IDE** — definition (chain skills, review at each step, context window carries artifacts); what it can do (full pipeline + manual eval + adversarial runs) vs. cannot (clean context per step, automatic eval gates, programmatic failure handling, unattended execution). |
| 5 | Exercise | Build a Bounded Agent: Full SDLC Pipeline in the IDE (30 min) — 10-step run of all four skills with eval script and adversarial agent at key points. |
| 6 | Lecture | **Context Window Discipline in a Bounded Agent** — **context window degradation pattern** (step 1 clean, step 4+ "falls off a cliff"); mitigations within the IDE (compact outputs, per-step evaluation, fresh-session workaround); the bounded agent's fundamental ceiling. |
| 7 | Lecture | **From Bounded Agent to Custom Harness** — **custom harness definition**: a Python program that calls the model API directly, passes artifacts between steps, runs eval scripts and adversarial agents per step, handles failures programmatically, and produces a scored final artifact; natural extension of Sessions 4–5. |
| 8 | Demo | Custom Harness: The Full Chain — instructor-led demo (API key required); clean context per step, automatic eval gates with retry/flag, adversarial checks, YAML artifacts (`stories.yaml` → `plan.yaml` → `review.yaml`) orchestrated between steps. |
| 9 | Compare/Contrast | **IDE Single-Step vs. Bounded Agent vs. Custom Harness** — three-column comparison across context handling, evaluation timing, artifact passing, failure handling, and human-in-the-loop. |
| 10 | Lecture | **The Intelligence OS (IIOS): Stage 3, Where You Are** — **IIOS stage framework**: Stage 2 (Off the Shelf) vs. Stage 3 (Task); the seven Stage 3 capabilities participants now have (RTCC, EC-first, Python evals, documented iteration, adversarial agents, deliberate invocation, bounded agents); the Stage 3 ceiling (everything personal). |
| 11 | Lecture | **Stage 4, What Comes Next** — Workflow stage requirements: automated harness/runner, guardrails between steps (adversarial + deterministic hooks), human punch-out points (bypass-tested), end-to-end success rate (95%/step → ~36% over 20 steps), audit trail, team + IT coordination; ~10x effort (~18h → ~172h); deferred to a future Stage 4 DLP. |
| 12 | Lecture | **Capstone: Artifact Showcase** — peer pairs present most-used skill (RTCC + evaluator + one improvement cycle), the evaluator itself, and one of {invocation-enabled skill, adversarial agent, bounded agent run}; partner question: "What would you do differently?" |
| 13 | Exercise | Capstone Artifact Showcase (30 min) — the paired presentation with discipline framing ("I iterated it N times and the evaluator showed…"). |
| 14 | Lecture | **Final Assessment + Commitment Statements** — repeat AI Adoption Maturity Assessment (DLP Completion signal: Dimensions 1–4 averaging 3.0+); **commitment statements**: out-loud, specific, observable next-sprint behavior ("I will [behavior] … I'll know I've done it when [artifact]"), with Week 12 Embedded Engineer follow-up. |
| 15 | Closing | Recap of the four goals per role; program ends, work continues. |
